articles.title: COP31 deadlock: Why countries failed to agree on fossil fuels, climate finance
articles.summary: From prolonged droughts and devastating wildfires to collapsing glaciers, extreme heat and rising sea levels, the climate crisis is no longer a distant
articles.body: From prolonged droughts and devastating wildfires to collapsing glaciers, extreme heat and rising sea levels, the climate crisis is no longer a distant warning. Its effects are being felt across continents, threatening livelihoods, disrupting ecosystems and putting millions of lives at risk.Yet, as the planet grapples with the mounting consequences of global warming, the countries expected to lead the fight are struggling to agree on a common course of action.This disconnect was evident at the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31), held in Antalya, Turkey, from November 9 to 20.Despite growing evidence of climate change, the summit ended without consensus on its central political agreement, the Antalya Pacts, exposing deep divisions over fossil fuels, climate finance and the responsibility of nations to pay for climate action.Co-hosted by Turkey and Australia, the negotiations became the longest-running climate talks in UN history.The final day was marked by heated exchanges over the omission of fossil fuel commitments and disagreements over financial assistance for developing countries. Some delegations walked out, while others accused oil-producing nations and developed countries of obstructing progress.The outcome has renewed questions about whether annual climate summits can deliver meaningful collective action at a time when the world is struggling to contain global warming.Despite the failure to agree on the central political declaration, countries made progress on several other issues, including climate finance mechanisms and a framework for a just transition.Here are eight key takeaways from COP31 and the major climate challenges that remain unresolved.1. Fossil fuel phaseout remains a major sticking pointOne of the biggest setbacks at COP31 was the failure of countries to agree on language concerning fossil fuels in the Antalya Pacts.The disagreement was significant because, at COP28 in Dubai in 2023, countries had agreed to transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems. However, three years later, they failed to reach a consensus on reaffirming or strengthening that commitment.The divide between countries pushing for a faster transition away from coal, oil and gas and those reluctant to make stronger commitments remained evident throughout the negotiations.Germany and several other European countries called for a global phaseout of fossil fuels. German environment minister Carsten Schneider had pushed for a commitment to a "global phaseout of fossil fuels". However, oil-producing nations, including Saudi Arabia, resisted stronger language.The final negotiations exposed the depth of these differences. EU representative Darragh O'Brien accused some oil-producing nations of obstructing progress, saying the talks had been "hijacked by some oil states".Russian delegate Sergei Kononuchenko, meanwhile, switched from Russian to English to directly address the EU delegation. He criticised developed countries for providing climate finance largely through loans to developing nations, describing it as "an old colonial distribution of labour under a new banner".Environmentalist Kavita Ashok said, "After reading the draft, it is very disheartening as an environmentalist to see that fossil fuels, the very issue the conference was meant to address, have been sidelined."Ashok said any transition away from fossil fuels must also account for the millions of people whose livelihoods depend on coal, petroleum and natural gas industries, particularly in countries such as India.She stressed the need to develop viable alternatives and ensure that the shift towards cleaner energy does not leave workers and communities behind."If we want to conserve fossil fuels, we need to look at alternatives, whether it is green energy, electric vehicles, solar power or hydroelectricity. There are so many forms of energy that can come into action," she told TOI.The failure to agree on fossil fuels has also raised concerns about the durability of earlier climate commitments. The inability to reaffirm the pledge made at COP28 highlights the growing difficulty of building consensus on more ambitious climate action, even as the urgency of reducing emissions increases.2. Climate finance: Developing countries still await clarityClimate finance was another major sticking point, with countries failing to agree on how much additional funding should be made available to help developing nations adapt to climate change.At COP29 in Baku, countries agreed to a new climate finance goal of at least $300 billion annually by 2035. At COP30 in Belém, Brazil, they agreed to triple adaptation finance to $120 billion annually by 2035, from a baseline of $40 billion.However, the interpretation and implementation of these commitments remain contested. At COP31, countries failed to agree on a clear additional funding figure for adaptation.The uncertainty over financial commitments also drew criticism from Ashok, who warned that any reduction in promised assistance would disproportionately affect vulnerable nations."The very will that existed for developed countries to help developing countries is being sidelined. Developing countries need that kind of aid and financial assistance to work on their climate change and global warming projects," she said.Referring to the $120-billion annual adaptation finance commitment, she questioned whether developing countries could rely on promises made at previous climate summits."If you diminish such a promise or trim the finances, countries in the Global South are really going to suffer," she said.The issue is particularly significant for developing countries, which face mounting costs from extreme weather events, rising temperatures and the need to strengthen infrastructure against climate-related risks.3. The world is preparing for life beyond 1.5°CCOP31 was the first climate summit since the United Nations warned that global temperatures were likely to exceed the 1.5°C threshold above pre-industrial levels within the next few years.The threshold is central to the 2015 Paris Agreement, under which countries committed to limiting global warming to well below 2°C while pursuing efforts to keep the rise to 1.5°C.The draft agreement at COP31 had acknowledged the likelihood of the world temporarily crossing the 1.5°C threshold and called for the overshoot to be kept as small and short-lived as possible. However, that recognition was lost after countries failed to agree on the central text.The United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) has warned that existing national climate commitments remain insufficient.If countries fully implement their current pledges, global temperatures could rise by up to 2.6°C. While this would represent an improvement over earlier projections of 3°C to 3.5°C, it would still expose communities and ecosystems to severe climate risks.Atmospheric greenhouse gas concentrations are also continuing to rise. According to the World Meteorological Organization, carbon dioxide levels reached a new record in 2025, while methane and nitrous oxide concentrations also hit record highs.The annual growth rate of atmospheric carbon dioxide has tripled since the 1960s, rising from an average of 0.8 parts per million (ppm) to 2.4 ppm between 2011 and 2020.Despite the worsening indicators, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has stressed that crossing the 1.5°C threshold does not mean the climate fight is over.4. Climate impacts and glacier loss demand urgent attentionThe consequences of rising temperatures are becoming increasingly visible, with extreme weather events threatening communities, infrastructure and livelihoods.Severe droughts, extreme heat, wildfires and falling water levels affected several parts of Europe during the summer. In August, flash floods triggered by a rock-ice avalanche in Nepal and Tibet washed away villages, killing more than 1,400 people and leaving thousands missing.Scientists have linked the disaster to rising temperatures and the destabilisation of mountain environments.An ICCI-UNEP report titled Overshoot and the Cryosphere warns that temporarily exceeding the 1.5°C warming threshold could accelerate the loss of glaciers and ice sheets, with consequences extending far beyond polar and mountain regions.James Kirkham, chief scientist at the International Cryosphere Climate Initiative and coordinating lead author of the report, told PTI that hundreds of millions of people could be affected by rising sea levels in the coming decades.He also warned that the loss of mountain glaciers could trigger water shortages, affecting agriculture, drinking water, irrigation and electricity generation. The risks are particularly significant for countries such as India and Nepal, where communities depend on Himalayan glaciers and seasonal snowmelt."It's a global problem, and it requires a global response to limit emissions, slow the rate of loss and build resilience, often across borders," he added.5. US absence highlights geopolitical divisionsThe United States was another notable absence at COP31, with the federal government not sending an official delegation for the second consecutive year.President Donald Trump's administration has distanced itself from international climate cooperation. The US withdrew from the Paris Agreement in January 2026 and formally notified the UN of its intention to leave the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change.However, American participation at the summit did not disappear entirely. A group of 18 Democratic members of the US House of Representatives travelled to Antalya, alongside other American political figures, including state and local leaders.Their presence followed the November midterm elections and was intended to maintain international contacts despite the federal administration's position.6. Renewable energy transition continues despite political deadlockDespite the failure to reach agreement on the central political declaration, the expansion of renewable energy continued to feature prominently in discussions outside the formal negotiations.The International Energy Agency's latest World Energy Outlook pointed to energy security as a major driver of the global transition. It said disruption to oil and gas supplies through the Strait of Hormuz had caused the biggest energy supply shock in history.Prolonged uncertainty over fossil fuel supplies could encourage countries to reduce their dependence on imported oil and gas and shift towards domestically generated electricity.The economics of clean energy have also changed, with solar panels, batteries and electric vehicles becoming increasingly competitive.At COP31, investment announcements and voluntary initiatives under the Action Agenda focused on electrification, shifting more energy use from fossil fuels to electricity."We are not entering the age of electricity, we have arrived at the age of electricity," Fatih Birol, head of the IEA, told the BBC. He said energy security and climate policies were now "closely aligned".However, accelerating the transition also requires governments to address policy barriers, infrastructure gaps and delays in obtaining permits.7. Climate leadership under scrutinyQuestions over the credibility of climate action extend beyond negotiating tables. Environmentalist Kavita Ashok criticised a contradiction between asking ordinary people to reduce their carbon footprints and the travel practices of world leaders attending climate summits."We have top leaders flying in their private jets. That is such a joke. If you are telling people to reduce their carbon footprint, even a layperson understands how to do it," she told TOI.Pointing to everyday measures such as carpooling and conserving energy, she questioned the message sent by leaders who arrive at climate conferences in private aircraft.8. COP31 exposes the limits of consensus, but is the process failing?While the failure to agree on the Antalya Pacts dominated the outcome, COP31 also saw progress on several other issues.Funds raised through a global carbon credit system will go towards helping developing countries adapt to climate change.Countries also agreed to advance a just transition framework designed to protect workers and communities as economies shift towards cleaner energy.As many as 164 other agenda items were discussed during the negotiations, some of which resulted in agreements.However, several issues remained unresolved and will now be taken up at COP32, including the work programme responsible for driving forward action on emissions cuts.The outcome has reignited the debate over the effectiveness of annual UN climate conferences.For three decades, the COP process has focused on building an international framework to tackle global warming. The Paris Agreement in 2015 marked a major diplomatic breakthrough, with countries committing to keep global warming well below 2°C and pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5°C.Subsequent summits delivered further commitments, including the establishment of a fund for climate-related loss and damage at COP27, a commitment to transition away from fossil fuels and triple renewable energy capacity at COP28, a new climate finance target at COP29 and increased support for adaptation at COP30.Offering a different perspective, Pradeep Singhvi, executive director, Energy and Climate, Grant Thornton Bharat, said COP31's failure to produce a headline political agreement did not necessarily mean global climate cooperation was weakening."Antalya will be remembered as a difficult COP. It ended without its headline political decision, while the proposed Antalya Pact did not include explicit language on transitioning away from fossil fuels. This may raise questions about the strength of global climate cooperation, but the underlying picture is more nuanced," he told TOI.Singhvi said reaching an agreement on shared climate goals was easier than deciding how individual countries should achieve them, given their differing economic circumstances and energy requirements."In my experience, agreeing on where we need to go is far easier than agreeing on how each of us gets there. The previous commitments have not gone away. What Antalya has shown is how much work it will take to put those commitments into practice," he said.He pointed out that some economies remained heavily dependent on energy revenues, while others were still working to provide affordable and reliable electricity to growing populations. For climate-vulnerable nations, the pace of the transition could have serious consequences."A common roadmap therefore requires more than stronger language. It requires confidence that countries can move ahead without compromising development or energy security, supported by finance and technology on practical terms," he said.Singhvi added that differences between countries were inevitable in a consensus-driven process, but accommodating these varied circumstances was also essential to the legitimacy of international climate agreements."The lesson from Antalya, in my view, is not that consensus has become unworkable. Rather, we cannot expect the final days of a COP to resolve differences that have accumulated over years," he said.He stressed that greater efforts were needed between climate summits, particularly on financing, implementation and the practical choices involved in transitioning away from fossil fuels."Ultimately, the strength of international climate cooperation will be judged not only by the agreements reached at COPs, but by the investment, technology and measurable progress they enable on the ground," he added.COP31 has once again exposed the difficulty of reconciling national interests with the need for collective climate action.While the summit failed to deliver agreement on some of the most contentious issues, the larger challenge remains unchanged: translating promises into action before the costs of global warming become even harder to contain.Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.title: A virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago left DNA that switches off a gene active in developing human brains, Lund University scientists found, a clue to what may make our brains different
articles.summary: Imagine that a virus which infected an animal millions of years ago could still have an influence on how its descendants develop, long after the infection
articles.body: Imagine that a virus which infected an animal millions of years ago could still have an influence on how its descendants develop, long after the infection itself had disappeared. While viruses are generally associated with illnesses and their ability to spread between individuals, their relationship with living organisms can become considerably more complicated when it comes to evolution. Some viruses leave behind traces of their genetic material, which become incorporated into the DNA of their hosts and can continue to be passed down through generations.A fascinating example of this has now emerged from research conducted by scientists at Lund University in Sweden, who have found that an ancient viral insertion in chimpanzee DNA switches off a gene that remains active in humans and plays a role in early brain development. According to a study published in Science Advances on October 23, 2026, this genetic difference could offer new insights into how human and chimpanzee brains have developed differently over millions of years.The research, titled “Retroviral insertions contributed to the divergence of human and chimpanzee brains” examines how an ancient viral infection may have influenced gene regulation in the two species, offering another perspective on the evolutionary changes that distinguish us from our closest living relatives.When viruses become part of our DNAHumans and chimpanzees share a remarkably similar genetic makeup, but this does not necessarily mean that the genes they carry are always used in the same way. Beyond the genes themselves, the way in which they are regulated, determining when they become active or are switched off, can also make a difference to how an organism develops.The researchers focused on a group of genetic sequences known as endogenous retroviruses. These are remnants of viruses that, during an infection, inserted their genetic material into the DNA of their hosts. When such an insertion occurs in germline cells, which give rise to reproductive cells, the viral sequence can become part of the genetic material inherited by subsequent generations.PTERV1, an ancient retrovirus that entered the chimpanzee lineage but is absent from the human genome, was also studied. Its genetic material appears at numerous locations within chimpanzee DNA. The researchers identified 158 PTERV1 insertions, which were associated with the formation of more than 150 species-specific heterochromatin domains.The team found that these viral insertions were heavily affected by a process called DNA methylation, a chemical modification that helps regulate gene activity. In simple terms, methylation can act like a switch, helping determine whether particular sections of DNA remain accessible for gene expression or become switched off.The gene studyAmong the viral insertions, the researchers identified one particularly significant sequence on chromosome 19 in chimpanzees. This insertion was found to silence a gene known as LINC00662, which produces a long non-coding RNA that is active in humans during early brain development.Long non-coding RNAs are known to influence how other genes and cellular processes behave. In this instance, LINC00662 appears to play an important role in neuronal development, particularly in the maturation of nerve cells and the growth of their extensions.To understand what was happening during brain development, the researchers used stem cells from both chimpanzees and humans to create brain organoids. These are small, three-dimensional structures grown in laboratories that resemble certain features of developing brain tissue. Although they are not fully functioning brains, they allow scientists to study aspects of early neural development under controlled conditions.Upon comparing the two, the team noticed that LINC00662 was strongly expressed in human brain organoids, whereas its activity was completely silenced in the chimpanzee models.The researchers then wanted to establish whether the viral insertion was actually responsible for this difference, rather than simply occurring alongside it. Using CRISPR-Cas9, a gene-editing technique that allows scientists to make targeted changes to DNA, they removed the PTERV1 sequence from chimpanzee cells. Following its removal, the expression of LINC00662 was restored in the chimpanzee cells.The developing brainThe team also investigated what happens when LINC00662 itself is switched off in human brain organoids. By using CRISPR to suppress its activity, they observed changes in the development of neuronal extensions, known as neurites, which are important for the formation of connections between nerve cells. These include axons, which carry signals away from nerve cells, and dendrites, which receive signals from other neurons. Both are important components of communication within the brain.However, the study does not establish that this single gene alone can explain the differences between chimpanzee and human brains, nor does it demonstrate that the viral insertion alone accounts for the evolution of human cognitive abilities.The findings essentially suggest that LINC00662 contributes to processes involved in the development and organisation of neural connections. Its absence or reduced activity could therefore influence aspects of how developing nerve cells mature.Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.title: Tesla and SpaceX assemble deal teams for a merger that could give Musk majority control
articles.summary: Tesla and SpaceX enlist directors and investments banks for their potential $3.5 trillion merger.
articles.body:
Tesla ( TSLA ) and SpaceX ( SPCX ) have enlisted five directors and three investment banks to help move forward what could be the biggest merger in history — and one that could give Elon Musk greater voting power than he currently has at Tesla.

The companies have tapped two directors from SpaceX and three from Tesla — Roelof Botha and Randy Glein from SpaceX, and Robyn Denholm, Kathleen Wilson-Thompson, and Jack Hartung from Tesla — to serve on two special committees overseeing the potential $3.5 trillion merger, the Financial Times reported .

Although all five have longstanding ties to Elon Musk, the CEO of both companies, they were deemed financially "disinterested" parties.

The committees have enlisted Morgan Stanley ( MS ) and Goldman Sachs ( GS ) for SpaceX and Evercore ( EVR ) for Tesla to develop financial models for the proposed all-stock merger. The exchange ratio — which will determine how much of the combined company existing Tesla and SpaceX shareholders will own — has yet to be agreed upon.

The deal, which could be reached before year's end, could give Musk something he's long sought: greater voting power than he currently has at Tesla. That could give Musk more latitude to pursue his ambitions in AI and robotics while diminishing other shareholders' ability to challenge his decisions.

Musk controls about 20% of Tesla's voting power, compared with 84% at SpaceX, where he holds supervoting shares. Depending on the terms of the deal and the governance structure of the combined company, Musk could end up with majority voting control.

articles.title: Why a Crusoe investor is betting on solar and batteries to power future AI data centers | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Next-generation data centers will need tens of gigawatts of power every year. One of Crusoe's investors thinks solar and energy storage are the obvious choice.
articles.body:
The problem of supplying power to AI data centers has become one of the central debates of the AI era. In just a few years, the U.S. grid has gone from basically zero growth to adding several gigawatts a year.

“Demand is growing faster than people appreciate,” Brook Porter, partner at G2 Venture Partners (G2VP), told TechCrunch. “It’s atoms, not bits, and the world is in the process of recognizing the realities of those challenges.”

It’s been a bumpy road. Because it takes a while to scale supply chains, companies have been securing power in any form they can. In many cases, that has meant buying, renting, and deploying natural gas power plants , but Porter thinks that hyperscalers and data center developers should look at the bigger picture if they want to move faster.

That picture involves solar paired with energy storage, based on an analysis Porter and his colleagues at G2VP recently conducted on the state of the data center power market.

“Global capacity of natural gas is only about 60 or 70 gigawatts per year, where solar is already at well over a terawatt,” he said. “Probably the most important lesson that we’ve learned over the last 20 years of backing companies is that Wright’s Law is the thing you want to leverage — making the same thing over and over again.”

Both solar and most forms of long-duration energy storage are built on small, modular technologies that can be manufactured at massive scale. “This is about speed and scale and economics, and we can win across all those dimensions,” Porter said.

G2VP had an early window into AI data center development, having led Crusoe’s Series C . “We’ve had a front-row seat at what’s been happening at that company, how they’ve evolved, how the different waves of data centers have evolved,” Porter said.

The venture firm estimates that data center investment will top $4 trillion until the end of the decade. As the next wave takes shape, the firm sees two different paths for data centers: small, on-grid facilities with their own generating capacity, and larger data centers powered by solar and long-duration energy storage.

“The big idea is to go off-grid,” Porter said. “What that would enable you to do is build with renewables in a way that’s independent of the grid. You can determine your own fate, go around some of the constraints of permitting, whether that’s access to the grid or air permits. You can accelerate your time to market dramatically.”

In recent years, energy storage has been synonymous with lithium-ion batteries, which are too expensive to compete with fossil fuels for round-the-clock power. But a new generation of long-duration energy storage products from the likes of Form Energy and G2VP portfolio company Antora Energy have brought the cost per megawatt-hour down significantly.

Even though the technologies might be a few years away from broad acceptance among data center developers, Porter said they should start thinking about them now.

“It’s analogous to surfing the biggest waves off of Mavericks here in Northern California. The wave is so big that you really have to be paddling and moving and be incredibly nimble to catch it. If you’re at a standstill, it’s just gonna blow you by,” he said.

articles.title: India’s space economy projected to rise to $40-45 billion by 2036: Minister Jitendra Singh
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: India's space economy is set for a major expansion, with its value projected to rise from nearly $9 billion at present to $40-45 billion by
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India's space economy is set for a major expansion, with its value projected to rise from nearly $9 billion at present to $40-45 billion by 2036, as private companies will be the key drivers of this growth, space, science and technology minister Jitendra Singh said on Tuesday.Addressing the 5th India International Space Conclave 2026 here, Singh said from a handful of startups some years ago, their number has gone up to nearly 400-500, showing the scale of expansion and transformation in the space sector over the past few years. He attributed the growth to a series of space reforms initiated under the leadership of PM Narendra Modi.The minister said the establishment of New Space India Limited (NSIL), the creation of the Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre (IN-SPACe), and the decision to open the space sector to private players marked a turning point in India's space journey. He cited Skyroot Aerospace's maiden launch vehicle flight, its multi-mission launch agreements and attainment of unicorn status, alongside advances by firms such as Agnikul, which are developing indigenous propulsion systems, rocket engines, earth-observation solutions and satellite imaging technologies.Singh called for greater corporate participation in scientific research, urging businesses to make better use of Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) funding and develop a stronger culture of philanthropy for science. “What you spend on research is also a worship,” he said, stressing that scientific research should receive greater support from private businesses.During a question-and-answer session at the event, the minister pointed out that India must continue to strengthen indigenous capabilities, with the guiding approach centred on indigenous sources, indigenous technology and indigenous projects, while remaining open to mutually beneficial international partnerships. “Investments from domestic private players have taken some time to pick up initially. articles.title: Why the US Army is about to blow up nearly 10,000 pounds of unstable explosives in Iowa
articles.summary: Plans to detonate an old stockpile of explosives could spread lead dust to surrounding communities.
articles.body: The US Army is moving ahead with plans to detonate the nation’s stockpile of lead azide at an ammunition plant in Middletown, Iowa, at approximately 9:00AM CST on Wednesday. The Verge reached out to experts on what to expect, and will keep this post updated. What material is the Army planning to detonate? There are 68 drums holding about 9,700 pounds of lead azide, an unstable chemical compound created to detonate munitions like grenades. The US started using lead azide as a primary explosive almost a century ago before “moving away” from it about 15 years ago because of how difficult the material is to store and transport, Robert Cekada, director of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), said in a Tuesday press briefing. At that point, the US transferred its remaining stockpile of lead azide to the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. Lead azide will explode at 350 degrees Celsius (662F). But it is also sensitive to flame, friction, or sudden shock, including fluctuations in temperature. Some of the material on site in Iowa is more than 60 years old. The material can crystallize as it degrades over time, becoming unstable enough to explode even at ambient temperatures. The Army noted some deterioration of the material in 2009 — but not any “dangerous crystallization” at the time, according to Cekada. The chemical was stored in liquid form, embedded in sawdust and burlap bags inside the drums. Water and ethanol were also added to the containers to keep the lead azide from freezing in the winter. But during a March inspection, Cekada said ATF noticed “significant crystallization on the exterior of the barrels.” That made the material too unstable for them to open the barrels to add more water and ethanol, Cekada said. Removing a lid might cause the barrels to detonate. Why is the Army detonating it now? Officials have been trying to figure out what to do with the crystallized lead azide since that alarming March inspection. The Army initially hired a contractor to safely dissolve the chemicals but canceled the contract earlier this year, according to reporting by The New York Times. Using a chemical neutralization agent “proved to be an unsafe method,” Army Col. Aaron Teller, commander of the 71st Explosive Ordinance Disposal Group, said at the Tuesday briefing, because crystallization on the outside of the barrels made it too risky to open the lids. “Everyone that we’ve spoken to through their experience has determined that this is the only safe path forward,“ Cekada said at the briefing. If they leave the chemicals as is, he said, they’re still at risk of exploding. “It’s not a matter of if, it’s a matter of when.” What are the risks? Compared to an uncontrolled, spontaneous explosion, a controlled detonation is supposed to limit the amount of lead dust unleashed on surrounding communities and the environment. Still, the dust plume could reach as far as 100 miles away from the site. The Army has released maps showing where lead dust is expected to travel based on its modeling. The last time the Army disposed of lead azide this way at a comparable scale was in 1977, according to Teller. At the time, they detonated 7,000 pounds of the material in Colorado in open air “with zero mitigation.” Even then, 75 percent of the lead particulate stayed on site, Teller said at the briefing. The Army now believes it can “significantly reduce” the spread of that last 25 percent of lead using walls made up of four 16,000-gallon water tanks to capture lead particulate and hopefully prevent it from escaping into the atmosphere. The 80-year-old earth-covered magazines holding the lead azide are cracked and deteriorating, Teller noted, and they are likely to break open after the detonation. To prepare, they’ve covered it with tarp and a special containment screen for lead. They also plan to flood it with 2 feet of foam to capture particulate pollution. Adam Telle, Acting Secretary of the Army, also said the Army has set out “state of the art gel blocks in huge quantities all around to ensure that we absorb as much of this blast as we possibly can.” Last week, the Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club sought a court order to stop the explosion from taking place, pending an Environmental and Health Impact Statement and an investigation into alternatives to detonating the material. President Donald Trump chimed in on social media, calling for a pause until a federal appeals court gave the Army the green light after previously granting a temporary stay. The court on Monday denied the emergency motion to stop the explosion, clearing the way for the Army to move forward. What precautions can people nearby take? The Iowa Department of Health and Human Services (Iowa HHS) recommends that anyone in potentially affected areas stay indoors and keep windows shut for 24 to 48 hours after the detonation. Iowa HHS also suggests switching off HVAC systems that might bring outdoor air inside or set them to modes that recirculate air, and using an air purifier with a HEPA filter. FEMA is helping relocate Middletown residents and others within a voluntary 5-mile evacuation zone. People who are pregnant, children, and individuals with chronic diseases should evacuate the affected areas, Sean Kaufman, principal deputy assistant secretary for preparedness and response at the Administration for Strategic Preparedness and Response, said at the briefing. “Outside of that area, if you’re close to that proximity and you’re uncomfortable, I think you need to do what you need to do to take care of your family,” Kaufman said. There is no “safe” level of exposure to lead, a neurotoxin that poses health risks when inhaled or ingested. Kids are at increased risk because their brains are still developing and are also more likely to touch contaminated surfaces and then stick their fingers in their mouths. But most adverse health effects — which can include fatigue and gastrointestinal upset alongside impacts on brain development — are connected to chronic lead exposure rather than as a result of a one-off event. “It is likely this exposure will not result in any observable acute clinical signs,” Will Sander, associate professor of preventive medicine and public health at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, says in an email to The Verge. “Overall, the risk is minimal, and there should be no long-term concerns.” What happens after the explosion? “The Army has done this before a long time ago and took lead measurements afterward that were low but hazardous (in my opinion),” Chris Kohler, an adjunct instructor at Indiana University who is an expert on hazardous waste, environmental remediation, and chemical hygiene, says in an email to The Verge. “The detonation will spread lead in the atmosphere. Not a desirable outcome.” Kohler and other experts say it’ll be important to continue monitoring the explosion site and surrounding areas to see if there needs to be any more remediation.

articles.title: FCC autoriza SpaceX a lançar 1 milhão de satélites para criar data centers no espaço | G1
articles.standfirst: Autorização é válida até 2040. Empresa de Elon Musk prevê iniciar os lançamentos em 2027 e acelerar a implantação dos satélites no ano seguinte.
articles.summary: Autorização da FCC é válida até 2040; empresa de Elon Musk prevê iniciar os lançamentos em 2027 e acelerar a implantação dos satélites no ano seguinte.
articles.body:
Starship, nave da Space, em foto divulgada em 23 de setembro de 2026 — Foto: Reprodução/SpaceX

Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

A Comissão Federal de Comunicações dos Estados Unidos (FCC, na sigla em inglês) autorizou nesta quarta-feira (25) a SpaceX , empresa de Elon Musk, a lançar até 1 milhão de satélites para criar data centers no espaço.

A autorização é válida até 2040 , segundo documento publicado nesta quarta no site do órgão regulador. A proposta faz parte do projeto Starmind , que prevê a instalação de satélites em órbita para formar centros de dados, estruturas que armazenam e processam informações.

A SpaceX tem a vantagem de contar com foguetes próprios , que já realizaram centenas de missões. Em agosto, Musk, CEO da empresa, prometeu fazer o primeiro lançamento no quarto trimestre de 2027 e acelerar a implantação dos satélites em 2028.

A empresa também firmou um acordo com a Nvidia , que fornecerá processadores de última geração Vera Rubin, desenvolvidos especialmente para operar no espaço.

No projeto Starmind, os satélites serão posicionados próximos uns dos outros, em uma região mais baixa da órbita terrestre, para garantir uma conexão estável. Eles também se comunicarão com os satélites da Starlink, outra rede da SpaceX, responsável pela transmissão dos dados.

A instalação de data centers no espaço tem algumas vantagens em relação às estruturas construídas em solo terrestre. Uma delas é a possibilidade de aproveitar melhor a energia solar. Em uma órbita chamada heliossíncrona, os satélites podem receber luz do Sol de forma contínua, com eficiência de captação de energia até oito vezes maior que a de uma instalação equivalente na Terra.

Desde o ano passado, aumentou o número de empresas interessadas em instalar data centers em órbita. Além da SpaceX, o Google desenvolve o programa Suncatcher , enquanto a Blue Origin apresentou à FCC um pedido de autorização para seu projeto Project Sunrise.

Outras empresas menores também têm iniciativas na área. A Starcloud , por exemplo, colocou em funcionamento um processador de última geração a bordo de um satélite no fim de 2025. Em outubro, o Google também alcançou um resultado semelhante.

articles.title: A robot submarine found evidence of an explosive volcanic eruption 20,170 feet below the Pacific near Mariana Trench; scientists say pyroclastic rocks are the deepest ever documented, in an unexpected zone
articles.summary: The oceans of the world have been the best keepers of secrets since the beginning of time itself.
articles.body: The oceans of the world have been the best keepers of secrets since the beginning of time itself. Not only have they been witnesses to the history of this Earth and its many species, but they also continue to hold buried evidence of a world that existed long before us, submerged beneath their vast waters. Only advanced technology can help humans unearth some of these mysteries.Scientists recently exploring the depths of the Pacific Ocean found evidence of explosive volcanic activity in an area where such activity was not expected to occur. According to a Frontiers report dated November 23, 2026, a remotely operated submarine, known as Jason/Medea, documented pyroclastic rocks at a depth of 6,148 metres (20,170 feet) near the Mariana Trench. The findings have been published in Frontiers in Earth Science.Exploring one of the deepest parts of the oceanThe Mariana Trench, situated in the western Pacific Ocean, is among the most fascinating geological features on the planet. Its deepest known section, the Challenger Deep, reaches approximately 10,935 metres below sea level, making it the deepest known point on the ocean floor. It was formed through the movement of tectonic plates over millions of years, and the trench is a reminder of how dramatically the Earth's surface can change beneath the oceans.There is, however, a reason why geologists are so intrigued by this region. The Pacific Plate is gradually moving beneath the Mariana Plate as part of a geological process known as subduction.It was in an effort to investigate these geological processes that researchers travelled to the Mariana Trench in late 2024 aboard the research vessel Thomas G. Thompson. Jason/Medea, a remotely operated vehicle (ROV), was deployed for this purpose as the team collected rock samples along the Challenger Deep Forearc Segment, an approximately 550-kilometre-long stretch of the seafloor. A total of seven dives across the region were carried out with the help of this submarine, allowing researchers to explore several underwater sections.Although the submarine could not descend to the very bottom of the Challenger Deep, its ability to reach depths of up to 6,500 metres allowed researchers to investigate the steep slopes and exposed geological formations along the trench wall.An unusual discoveryThe rocks recovered by the researchers included pyroclastic deposits, which are formed when volcanic eruptions fragment and eject material such as ash, rock and other volcanic debris. These materials can accumulate and settle into layers, sometimes forming solid rock as they cool and become compacted. On land, pyroclastic flows are commonly associated with explosive volcanic eruptions, in which hot material travels rapidly away from an eruption site.The researchers identified thin, flat layers of volcanic rock, along with various patterns and fractures that suggested the material had previously moved across the seafloor as hot pyroclastic flows. Some of the rock formations had retained sufficient heat during the process to fuse together again as they cooled.Dr Robert J. Stern of the University of Texas at Dallas, the lead author of the research, described the discovery as unexpected, noting that explosive volcanism near ocean trenches is unusual. The research, published in Frontiers in Earth Science on November 23, 2026, identifies these as the deepest pyroclastic rocks documented to date.What makes their location even more interesting is that the forearc, the geological region between the trench and the volcanic arc, is generally considered too cool for the mantle beneath it to melt easily. Consequently, the presence of relatively young volcanic rocks so close to the trench has raised new questions about the geological processes taking place beneath the region.How does volcanic activity work under such immense pressure?Underwater volcanic eruptions are not unusual, but the conditions at these depths make the process considerably different from what scientists observe on land or in shallow waters. Gases trapped within magma can expand rapidly when pressure decreases near the surface, contributing to explosive eruptions. However, at depths of more than 6,000 metres, the water above the seafloor exerts immense pressure, which significantly restricts the expansion of gases released from rising magma.Furthermore, the researchers have suggested that the volcanic activity observed in the Mariana region may have involved supercritical fluids. These are substances that exist under extremely high temperatures and pressures, beyond their critical points, where they no longer behave like ordinary liquids or gases.These fluids are believed to potentially explain why the eruptions were less explosive than comparable volcanic activity closer to the surface, while still producing fragmented volcanic material and hot flows. Scientists are still studying the precise mechanisms behind this unusual form of deep-sea volcanism.The researchers have also observed differences between the eastern and western sections of the forearc, with older mantle rocks being more noticeable in the east and younger volcanic rocks in the west. This suggests that the two sections may be undergoing different geological processes. However, further sampling and radiometric dating of the rocks are needed to confirm this hypothesis.Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.title: Hera spacecraft investigates damage at asteroid "crash scene"
articles.summary: The mission is studying an asteroid deliberately knocked off course by a colliding spacecraft.
articles.body:
A spacecraft has arrived at an asteroid to investigate the damage caused by an unprecedented cosmic crash.

In what may sound like the plot of a disaster movie, Nasa's Dart spacecraft deliberately smashed into the space rock in 2022 to knock it off course.

The Nasa craft was obliterated on impact. Four years on, a European Space Agency (ESA) mission, called Hera, is scouring the scene to fully assess the aftermath of the collision - with the first images set to be released later on Wednesday.

The asteroid poses no threat, instead this was the first ever test of our planetary defences to see what action we could take if a space rock was heading for our planet.

"Hera is a sort of Inspector Columbo going back to the crash scene to investigate what is the outcome of this impact," said Patrick Michel, principal investigator of ESA's Hera mission.

The crash test focussed on a pair of asteroids: a larger one called Didymos - about 730m (2,400ft) wide - which is orbited by a smaller rock called Dimorphos, about 150m (490ft) wide.

The Dart spacecraft targeted Dimorphos, hurtling into the rock at 22,000km per hour (14,000mph). Images beamed back showed the asteroid's rocky surface coming ever closer until the feed cut out on impact.

It was such a big smash-up that the trail of debris, measuring about 10,000km long (6,200 miles), was spotted by telescopes on Earth and in space.

The crash showed it was possible to change the path of the smaller asteroid.

Before the collision it took Dimorphos 11 hours and 55 minutes to orbit around Didymos. After the Dart crash, the duration of its orbit had shrunk by about 33 minutes.

But the arrival of the second spacecraft, Hera, will help scientists to answer many more questions.

"Dart exploded in the asteroid, and therefore we don't have the information of what is its final state," explained Michel.

"The impact could have left a crater - and if it is the case, we need to understand the size and the depth. Or [the impact] may have entirely reshaped the asteroid."

The Hera mission will spend the next year studying Dimorphos, and take a look at Didymos too.

The spacecraft is packed with instruments, and it also has two small shoe-boxed sized satellites onboard, which can study the impact site up close, and then later land on the asteroid.

A key task is to measure the mass of Dimorphos, to work out how effective the spacecraft's shove was.

This information would be vital if we ever spotted a space rock that was on a collision course with Earth.

"It would help us to predict what would happen if we had to hit another asteroid," said Prof Simon Green, a planetary scientist who is on Hera's science team.

"We [could] measure its properties and say: 'Well, we need this mass of spacecraft, travelling at this speed, this early, in order to deflect it enough so that it misses the Earth'."

Asteroids pose a significant threat to our planet.

The biggest, which measure more than a kilometre across, could cause global devastation. But medium-sized asteroids around the same dimensions as Dimorphos could wipe out a city.

"We all know what happened to the dinosaurs, right? And we don't want that to happen to us," said Carolyn Ernst, Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory, who works on both the Dart and Hera missions.

"The good news for us is that there are far fewer potential threats out there in the Solar System than there were millions of years ago. But there are objects out there."

She said the biggest asteroids have been spotted, and none are heading to Earth.

"The smallest stuff isn't too much of a threat because our atmosphere protects us," she added.

"But there's a size range in the middle where we don't know where all of them are, and it could, if impacted, cause problems for humanity. And if we can find out about that and know about that, well, we sure as heck would want to try to stop that."

Scientists want to gather as much intelligence as they can about space rocks - to make us as well equipped as possible to deal with whatever the Universe throws at us.

A new mission is launching in 2027 to track potentially hazardous asteroids: a space telescope called the Near-Earth Object (NEO) Surveyor.

There are also more visits planned to asteroids, including to one called Apophis, which is about 450m (1,480ft) long.

Apophis was discovered in 2004 and it was initially thought it might hit the Earth as early as 13 April 2029.

But now scientists understand its orbit better, and say it won't hit us for at least the next 100 years. Instead of a crash in 2029, it will fly just 32,000km (20,000 miles) above our surface.

This will give scientists the rare chance to study a space rock up-close.

Two spacecraft will head to Apophis, including Nasa's Osiris-Apex (which previously grabbed a sample from another asteroid called Bennu) and Ramses, a joint mission between ESA and the Japanese Space Agency (JAXA).

articles.title: Pak astronaut Ali reaches China’s Tiangong station
articles.summary: BENGALURU: Pakistan’s first astronaut to travel to space, Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, reached China’s Tiangong space station Wednesday, over three hours after
articles.body: BENGALURU: Pakistan’s first astronaut to travel to space, Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, reached China’s Tiangong space station Wednesday, over three hours after the Shenzhou-24 spacecraft lifted off at 5.48 am (IST) aboard a Long March-2F rocket.The docking, confirmed by the China Manned Space Agency (CMSA), marks the first time a foreign astronaut has joined a crewed mission to China’s space station and the first joint crewed flight involving Chinese and foreign astronauts in its human spaceflight programme.Shenzhou-24, carrying Ali and Chinese astronauts Tang Hongbo and Wu Yi, separated from the rocket about 10 minutes after launch and entered its designated orbit. CMSA declared the launch a complete success and said the astronauts were in good condition.The spacecraft subsequently completed its rendezvous and docking with Tiangong, where the incoming joined astronauts who were already aboard the station. The mission is part of China’s regular space-station operations and crew rotation programme.Ali is serving as a payload specialist and will undertake a short-duration stay. Besides participating in routine crew activities, he will work on joint China-Pakistan space science experiments, including the installation of experimental samples and equipment. Four collaborative projects in biotechnology and materials are planned, with Ali also scheduled to conduct an in-orbit experiment involving photosynthetic cyanobacteria.The mission is the outcome of an agreement signed by China and Pakistan in Feb 2025 covering astronaut selection, training and participation in Chinese space-station missions. Following a three-stage selection process, two Pakistani candidates were shortlisted and trained in China. Ali was selected for the flight, with the other candidate retained as backup.After completing the short-term mission, Ali will return to Earth aboard Shenzhou-23 alongside two members of its crew, Zhang Zhiyuan and Li Jiaying.The Shenzhou-24 mission also has an unusual crew-rotation arrangement. Chinese astronaut Zhu Yangzhu, who is currently aboard Tiangong, will remain in orbit for a year-long stay experiment, becoming China's first astronaut to undertake a year-long orbital mission. The two other Shenzhou-24 astronauts, Tang and Wu, will remain aboard the station for approximately six months.CMSA said more than 90 scientific experiments and technology tests are planned during the mission, covering space life sciences, materials science, microgravity physics, space medicine and new space technologies.For Pakistan, Ali’s arrival marks its entry into human spaceflight. For China, it is the first operational demonstration of its ambition to open Tiangong to international participation.Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.title: Researchers have developed a rewritable display that can retain an image for months without electricity; the new material could eventually make electronic displays far more energy-efficient
articles.summary: Screens rule our world today, we usually begin our day with them and most often, end with a screen too.
articles.body: Screens rule our world today, we usually begin our day with them and most often, end with a screen too. Between that time, most of us barely look away from a screen, it could be a laptop or a phone, you must be reading the article on a screen too. The prevalence of screens has also made a lot of us curious about what goes behind their working. Every one of those screens is working constantly, even when the picture isn't changing. Hold a still image on your phone and the display keeps spending energy to maintain it, frame after frame.A team in Australia has built a display that doesn't do that. It holds a picture with no power at all, and not just for a few minutes.The koala that wouldn't fadeResearchers at the ARC Centre of Excellence for Transformative Meta-Optical Systems (TMOS), working across RMIT University and the Australian National University, reported a reflective display that can keep an image for months with no electricity. They drew a map of Australia, the TMOS logo and a koala to test their research.The koala was left sitting under ordinary room conditions for three months without any noticeable change. Lead researcher Dr Phuong Yen Le told Mirage News that the koala is still in her possession and "it still looks the same a year later."A material that can change its mindThe new form display is made from materials called phase change materials, or PCMs. Specifically, antimony selenide (Sb₂Se₃) was used for this project. Most materials are stuck in one atomic arrangement once they're made. PCMs can be nudged back and forth between a tidy, crystal-like order and a jumbled, glassy one, over and over.The two states interact with light differently. Light moves through them at different speeds and is absorbed to different degrees, so they look different. By combining those two phases with different thicknesses of the material, the team produced colours ranging from deep blues through greys to oranges.The other key property is that antimony selenide is "non-volatile". This helps it settle into a phase, which then stays there. Nothing needs to keep feeding it power, which is the difference from the screen in your pocket.Drawing with light, erasing with heatUnlike your usual pencil of charcoal and eraser of rubber, the pen used here is a laser which can be erased in an oven.To wipe the screen, the material is heated evenly to roughly 200°C. At that temperature the atoms have enough energy to shuffle around and settle into their most stable arrangement, which is the orderly crystal. This process is called annealing, and it leaves a clean blank canvas.To draw, co-author Dr Shvedov fires short laser pulses at the surface. Each pulse gives a tiny region just enough energy to scramble its atoms, then cools so quickly that they freeze mid-scramble before they can tidy themselves back into crystals. Those frozen-in-disorder regions show up as different colours. The researchers compare the process to turning glass into quartz and back again, repeatedly. After erasing, the team found no leftover ghost image, even under a 5× magnification microscope.The early work to a revolutionThe research, while quite remarkable, is early stage work. Firstly, the setup requires a laser to write which is not a mass-produced accessible technology. Dr. Le says the device ultimately needs to be fully electrical, and she's now testing the material's electrical characteristics to get there.While the research has displayed impeccable results with a wide colour gamut, Dr. Le acknowledges that the project is able to give only a limited range of colors for now. Getting more colours will probably mean changing the device's structure, and that's the next puzzle on her list.Why it's worth caring aboutThe appeal is in what a screen like this could eventually be used for. Anything that shows the same image for long stretches is where the technology can be utilised, for instance, signage, labels, e-reader-style displays. There, the energy goes into maintaining a picture that rarely changes, and a display that only draws power when the image is rewritten could cut that to nearly nothing. The researchers frame reflective displays as an emerging, more sustainable alternative with near-zero power draw while holding an image.Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.title: Canadian astronaut welcomes baby girl from space station
articles.summary: Joshua Kutryk, currently on his first space mission, is just the fourth astronaut in history to miss the birth of a child while aboard the International Space Station.
articles.body:
A Canadian astronaut aboard the International Space Station is celebrating the birth of his third child from hundreds of miles above Earth.

Joshua Kutryk and his wife, Heather Kutryk, welcomed their daughter as the astronaut takes part in a six-month space mission that began in October, the Canadian Space Agency announced on Tuesday.

"Even with the distance between us, we feel incredibly connected as we welcome our new little star into our lives," said the couple in a statement shared by the agency.

Joshua Kutryk, currently on his first space mission, is just the fourth astronaut in history to miss the birth of a child while aboard the International Space Station.

The couple have two older children, aged five and seven.

"We are very proud of our growing family and are looking forward to getting our little crew of five all reunited."

In a statement, the couple said that Joshua's spaceflight was a "childhood dream" come true.

"We hope to show our children that big dreams are worth pursuing, that hard work and determination matter, and that with the support of family and a strong community, extraordinary things are possible," they said.

Prior to becoming an astronaut, Kutryk, from Fort Saskatchewan, Alberta, was a fighter pilot and a colonel in the Royal Canadian Air Force. He was recruited by the Canadian Space Agency in 2017.

Kutryk was the only Canadian selected to be part of NASA's SpaceX Crew-13 mission, where four astronauts are conducting scientific experiments and testing new technologies in space.

The crew also includes two US astronauts, Luke Delaney and Jessica Watkins, and one Russian astronaut, Sergey Teteryatnikov.

Before their take off on 1 October, Heather Kutryk told Canada's public broadcaster CBC News that her family had been preparing for years before the mission, saying it was "a long time coming".

Heather added that her pregnancy was "not exactly planned" but that it was "a great thing".

"I'm not that stressed out. I feel like we have a really good community. I feel well supported by both CSA and Nasa," she said.

"It's six months, I feel like we'll be fine."

In a separate interview with BBC's US news partner CBS News, Joshua Kutryk said he hopes his new child will look at her dad's mission as "making some sacrifice, taking some risk, but doing so in the name of public service and the name, in my case, for Canada."

articles.title: FCC signs off on SpaceX’s plan to put up to 1 million data center satellites into space
articles.summary: The FCC has authorized SpaceX’s plans to put up to 1 million AI data centers into space through its “Starmind” initiative.
articles.body: In an announcement on Wednesday, the FCC says it authorized SpaceX to deploy up to 1 million AI chip-equipped satellites as part of the Elon Musk-owned company’s “Starmind” initiative. With several others also pursuing the idea of putting AI data centers in space, including Google and Blue Origin, this is the first approval the agency has granted for a full “constellation” of AI satellites. The FCC’s approval requires SpaceX to deploy at least one satellite by 2033, and meet the 1 million satellite milestone by 2040. The FCC also deferred SpaceX’s request to dispose of satellites located above 600km in space “graveyard” orbits, rather than having them burn up in the Earth’s atmosphere, saying the company hasn’t provided “sufficient information” about its disposal process plans. SpaceX has described its Starmind project as a way to “capture solar energy in space to power” AI capabilities on Earth. The company says Starmind will transmit data to Earth using high-speed lasers that connect to Starlink. It plans to produce chips for its satellites at an upcoming Terafab facility. Google has already taken its first steps toward putting compute into space, with the launch of a “Project Suncatcher” AI server satellite last month. Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin will carry out the first dedicated heavy-lift launch for Project Suncatcher in 2029.

articles.title: The loneliest peptide party in New York
articles.summary: In this week’s Optimizer, an inside look at a peptide launch party in New York and how the peptide curious are looking for more information.
articles.body: This is Optimizer, a weekly newsletter sent from Verge senior reviewer Victoria Song that dissects and discusses the latest gizmos and potions that swear they’re going to change your life. Opt in for Optimizer here. On a rainy fall evening, an experimental art venue in Chelsea Market had a small line out the door. There are always lines in New York City. Viral food trends, gallery exhibitions, pop-ups, and parties. The folks in line looked like your average joe, ready for a Friday night on the town. You wouldn’t look twice — except, perhaps, for a man with a wizard beard and a laser sword strapped to his back. Inside, the man with a laser sword stood in the middle of the cavernous bottom floor of a two-story warehouse strewn with large bean bags. On the wall were psychedelic projections of jellyfish, shrimp, and other sea creatures. A bizarre choice, considering peptides won’t induce any trippy vision quests, and not a single person was getting groovy. The industrial beams had posters with QR codes that you could scan to get samples of Afterglow, a new type of peptide product. According to seemingly discarded pamphlets around the venue, Afterglow isn’t a standard injectable or oral peptide. The company makes strips that dissolve under the tongue. The “Afterglow Peptide Field Guide” also described what each sample does, dosing recommendations, and potential side effects. At the upstairs bar, bartenders mixed custom cocktails called Afterburn — complete with bioluminescent veggie nectar — and Margatrutide. (For the record, a bioluminescent veggie nectar cocktail tastes as awful as you think.) Welcome to a peptide launch party. [Image: Bioluminescent veggie nectar cocktails for the peptide curious. Peptide parties are old news in San Francisco, but they’re somewhat more novel in New York City. Milling around the edges of the venue were various reporters and photographers. We were all trying to get a sense of why anyone had bothered to come out. Not that many did. Despite the venue’s size, the main floor had plenty of empty space. One person I spoke to was a fencer with sore joints. They’d heard that one of the peptides might help with recovery. Another had a father in the wellness industry and had heard vague things about how effective peptides could be. One woman, staring at a projected jellyfish, merely shrugged. Her friend was more into “wellness stuff” and she had no plans, so, why not check out a party? A man, staring into his bag of Afterglow samples, was mostly interested in weight loss but scared about the safety of gray market products. A few feet away, another man was furiously reading the Afterglow pamphlet. “I like to know what I put in my body,” he said. The only problem was he didn’t remember which sample he had tried. A common refrain: Well, this beats doing research online. This, at least, was a social event where you could theoretically connect with other people. And there were clusters of strangers speaking to each other. Mostly, near the bar. Everywhere else, people stared awkwardly on their phones, their eyes occasionally roaming the room without meeting anyone else’s gaze for more than a second or two. After a while, they’d disappear into the back room and reappear with a goody bag full of peptide samples. [Image: Scanning a QR code got you one of two goodie bags at the Afterglow launch peptide party. After 90 minutes, I decided to leave. For the umpteenth time that evening, I’d walked up to someone, asked about peptides, and got a noncommittal “I really don’t know anything — I just came to learn more.” (When asked if they had, they invariably shrugged and pointed to the goody bag.) It was clear that the only peptide evangelists here were likely associated with the launch. The whole thing, to me, seemed as if someone had tried to draw a cool party from memory. The last thing I saw was a person draped in a ghost sheet sitting alone in the corner. As it turned out, the man with the laser sword was a performance artist who’d been invited to attend. Out of journalistic integrity, I asked if he had ever tried peptides. He told me he was more interested in the unifying energy of the universe. When I got up to leave, he waved and said, “Giggles.” If I were peptide curious, the Afterglow launch party was a pretty awful way to learn anything about these substances. To be fair, Afterglow’s Partiful invitation mostly described this event as “an environment great for aura farming” and the “hard launch of [its] first of many experiments in culture.” Nevertheless, as part of the press, I did walk away with a smattering of Afterglow’s products. In total, I got packets of what Afterglow calls Charge (NAD+), Rejuvenate (glutathione), Wolverine Blend (BPC-157 / TB-500), Strength Blend (CJC-1295 / Ipamorelin), Glow Blend (GHK-Cu / BPC-157 / TB-500), Connect (PT-141), GLP-2 (tirzepatide), and GLP-3 (retatrutide). Or at least that’s what the packaging says. There’s no way to truly verify gray market peptides for safety or efficacy because they’re unregulated products. First of all, last I checked, GLP-1 medications do not upgrade like iPhone models. Afterglow’s pamphlet correctly lists that your body has “three hormone switches”: GLP-1, GIP, and glucagon. The accompanying descriptors of what each does are broadly correct, though lacking in nuance. For example, there is a hormone called glucagon-like peptide 2, but it’s not tirzepatide. The “real” GLP-2 is a hormone related to intestinal health. Tirzepatide is still considered a GLP-1 medication that’s a dual agonist because it works on two hormones (GLP-1 and GIP.) The GLP-2 moniker is a misnomer popularized by ill-informed influencers. The same goes for retatrutide, which, as of this writing, is still an unapproved GLP-1 medication that works on three hormones (GLP-1, GIP, and glucagon) and is therefore a triple agonist. There is no such thing as GLP-3. [Image: Most partygoers didn’t know a single thing about peptides and had to read the provided pamphlets. For all the samples, there were no instructions regarding dosing on the packaging — just another QR code leading to Afterglow’s product page. Those pages happen to contain instructions for how to use the strips, and the amount of product within the strips. There are disclaimers about how little studied the compounds are, but nothing about interactions, side effects, or what to expect while taking. Just a throwaway line to talk to your doctor. All that information, you’d have to find on the pamphlet given at the party. (Ironically, some “important cautions” on the pamphlet state to avoid taking samples with alcohol, at a party where the booze was flowing.) Provided you didn’t throw it out. One would hope that information is on a box if you were to buy directly from the seller. But for all intents and purposes, what I just described is what a clueless partygoer would have to go on. If everything in that pamphlet were 100 percent factual, perhaps a conscientious partygoer could feel reassured. On that front, I have bad news. The pamphlet calls PT-141 an “FDA-approved peptide that boosts sexual desire for both men and women.” [Image: Several free samples were available at Afterglow’s peptide party. PT-141, also known as bremelanotide or Vyleesi, is FDA approved. But only for premenopausal women suffering from hypoactive sexual desire disorder. It is not approved for post-menopausal women, men, or for general sexual performance enhancement. Another concern: How does one evaluate a sublingual peptide strip? Specifically, is this delivery method even scientifically proven effective in humans? Spoiler: It’s not! A collapsible FAQ menu on Afterglow’s site states, “We don’t know yet. Nobody has published how much of most peptides reaches the blood from a strip compared with an injection. We’re funding studies to measure exactly that, and we’ll share what we find.” As for why you’d want to even try a sublingual strip? Afterglow’s website suggests it’s more convenient than injections or pills. No refrigeration, no needles, and no need for learning how to reconstitute a drug. Just pop a strip under the tongue and go. And good luck trying to find reputable sources of information on your own. Afterglow says it’s funding its own research, but its site has no reviewable documentation just yet. A Google search brings up a questionable AI overview, a handful of links from dubious med spas, a couple of dead links, and one PubMed study in mice. Most of the links also primarily discuss the difference between oral peptides in pill form and injectables — so not terribly relevant here. I’d consider it fair game if I were confident that anyone at the party I went to did their due diligence. As it stands, I talked with over a dozen people who were mostly there for vibes, booze, and freebies. Not all peptide parties are created equal. Some happen on WWII cargo ships, complete with panel discussions about peptide supply chains. Another “peptide 101” talk I attended in New York happened at the back of a bitcoin bar. There, most attendees also knew very little about peptides, but at least they got treated to a PowerPoint presentation about the basics. There was a dubious demonstration of how to inject oneself that would’ve probably made any pharmacist or doctor scream. But at the very least, peptides were defined and attendees could ask questions. (The answers to those questions were on the right track with regard to the dangers of the gray market. They were less reliable about scientific rigor and why “anecdotal evidence” is not the same as clinical evidence of safety.) [Image: A performance artist wearing a laser sword bid me farewell by saying, “Giggles!” He told me he was not familiar with peptides. But a striking, recurring theme is just how much is unknown. These substances aren’t well-studied in humans, so there’s not much evidence as to long-term benefits or side effects. The peptide curious know shocking little about the substances they’re supposedly interested in. Likewise, it’s incredibly difficult to get reliable, unbiased data on gray market interest or usage, though there have been attempts to quantify this surging demand in recent months. Case in point, telehealth provider Hims & Hers just conducted a consumer survey of roughly 2,000 American adults. Of those surveyed, 68 percent said they had little to no knowledge about peptides. Less than 18 percent were even able to identify that peptides are chains of amino acids. Even so, 40 percent said they were interested or very interested in trying injectable prescription treatments — including peptides — if offered by a telehealth service. Even so, peptides are everywhere. The word appears in copious ads for skincare creams, weight loss drugs, and supplements. Looksmaxxers, influencers, and celebrities like Gwyneth Paltrow and Joe Rogan talk about them in podcasts, documentaries, and social media as if they’re miracle shortcuts. Hims & Hers has even announced it’s launching a service called Peptide Plus — nevermind that the vast majority of what it’ll offer are not actual peptides. [Image: The last sight I saw before leaving the party. In this kind of environment, of course more people will become peptide curious. Which makes it even more concerning that the most readily available information sources are not medical or scientific experts well-versed on the topic at hand. There are dubious links online summarized into less-than-critical AI overviews. There are pamphlets handed out at weird parties, where there’s more booze and schmooze than education. Influencers branding themselves as experts as they flash crudely summarized studies in a bar back room. Industry panels that are inaccessible to the average consumer, full of jargon and assumed knowledge of the science at hand. It’s clear something needs to be done until general knowledge improves. Until then, the parties will continue.

articles.title: SpaceX stock pares losses following FCC approval for data centers in space
articles.summary: The FCC authorized SpaceX to deploy up to 1 million data center satellites.
articles.body:
The FCC authorized SpaceX ( SPCX ) to deploy up to 1 million data center satellites , calling it "the first authorization in US history for a constellation of data centers in space."

SpaceX first made the request in January for what it said would be the "first step toward becoming a Kardashev II-level civilization — one that can harness the Sun's full power."

The approval helped SpaceX pare some of its losses from earlier in the day amid a broader tech sell-off and investor concerns over a potential merger with Tesla ( TSLA ). The stock is currently down around 1%, compared with 8% earlier in the day.

In response to a post on Elon Musk-owned X by FCC Chair Brendan Carr, Musk replied, "This will be a great asset to America and the world."

The project is a long way from proven. SpaceX has warned investors in its IPO filing that orbital compute rests on technology "not yet been proven at commercial scale, or at all," adding that it could be ultimately unsuccessful. CFO Bret Johnsen said in September that SpaceX is targeting its first orbital compute satellites next year, with a much bigger push in 2028.

SpaceX also hasn't announced any customers for orbital capacity. Its AI revenue today comes from on-site data centers.

Wood Mackenzie estimated that a hypothetical 1-gigawatt orbital data center would cost about $170 billion, more than three times that of a ground-based one, owing largely to the expense of launching it from Earth. The firm said launch costs would need to fall about 70% to be competitive.

SpaceX spent $19.6 billion on capital expenditure in the third quarter , nearly triple what it spent a year earlier and more than its $14.6 billion in revenue. Most of that spending went to AI. The company expects capital spending to roughly double to $35 billion to $40 billion in the fourth quarter as it expands its AI computing capacity.

articles.summary: Elon Musk hails FCC’s approval of SpaceX’s Starmind project as ‘a  great asset to America and the world.’
articles.body:
The United States ⁠⁠Federal ⁠⁠Communications Commission (FCC) has authorised Elon Musk’s ⁠⁠SpaceX to deploy a constellation of data centres in space, named “Starmind”, in a bid to help meet rapidly ‌‌growing demand ‌‌for AI computing.

The FCC said on Wednesday the approval marked a first in the history of the United States.

“At this pivotal time in America’s development of super intelligence [artificial intelligence], the FCC is granting SpaceX authorisation to deploy 1,000,000 orbital compute modules to process massive amounts of data to be used back here on Earth,” an FCC press release said.

“This action opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth,” said FCC Chairman Brendan Carr in a statement.

Elon Musk praised the FCC decision on social media.

“Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world,” he said on X .

Approving the application will permit SpaceX “to pioneer emergent ‌technology that advances American leadership in space and artificial intelligence”, the FCC said.

Data centres are the physical backbone of artificial intelligence, requiring massive amounts of power.

SpaceX filed for permission to deploy Starmind ‌earlier this year.

It was unclear whether SpaceX would put 1 ⁠million satellites in space, where only 17,000 satellites exist currently. Satellite ⁠operators sometimes request approval for higher numbers of satellites than they intend to deploy to buy design flexibility.

SpaceX sought approval for 42,000 Starlink satellites before it began deployment of that system. The growing network currently has ⁠just more than 11,000 satellites in space.

Last month, the FCC’s Space Bureau and Wireless Telecommunications Bureau granted Space Exploration Holdings, LLC, a subsidiary of SpaceX, authority to launch and operate the SpaceX NGSO MSS System, commercially known as Starlink.

Amazon’s rival satellite unit Leo ⁠and others have criticised the plan, suggesting SpaceX was unlikely to deploy all the satellites and that it could take centuries to do so.

“Amazon should focus on ‌getting Amazon’s house in order with their own launches and their own satellite constellation, rather than worrying about other people that are actually out there launching satellites at the ‌pace ‌and cadence that SpaceX is,” Carr said.
