articles.title: Images of asteroid targeted to test Earth's defences reveal stadium-sized crater
articles.summary: The asteroid's surface was transformed after a spacecraft was deliberately crashed into it four years ago
articles.body:
The first images of an asteroid that Nasa deliberately crashed into have revealed a stadium-sized crater on its surface.

The extensive damage was caused when a Nasa spacecraft hit the asteroid Dimorphos in 2022. The asteroid posed no threat, but this was a test of our planetary defences to see if it was possible to knock a space rock off course.

Four years on, a European Space Agency (ESA) spacecraft called Hera is scouring the scene to fully assess the aftermath of the collision.

"The crater is almost as large as the body itself, which is really, really spectacular," said Dr Sabina Raducan, a planetary scientist, who is on the Hera science team.

"It's hard to describe in words all the excitement to actually finally see what happened. And as a crater person, I can also say it's beautiful."

The original 2022 crash test was carried out by a Nasa spacecraft called Dart which hurtled into Dimorphos at 14,000mph (22,000km/h).

It was such a big smash-up that the trail of debris, measuring about 6,200 miles long (10,000km), was spotted by telescopes on Earth and in space.

Dimorphos is about 150m (500ft) wide and was partly chosen as the target because it is one of an asteroid pair - it orbits around a larger space rock called Didymos, which is about 730m (2,400ft) wide.

The crash showed it was possible to change the path of the smaller asteroid.

Before the collision, it took Dimorphos 11 hours and 55 minutes to orbit around Didymos. After the crash, the duration of its orbit had shrunk by about 33 minutes.

Watch: Moment Nasa spacecraft leaves stadium-sized crater in asteroid

A key objective of the Hera mission is to measure the mass of Dimorphos, in order to work out how effective the spacecraft's shove was.

This information would be vital if we ever spotted a space rock that was on a collision course with Earth.

"It would help us to predict what would happen if we had to hit another asteroid," said Prof Simon Green, a planetary scientist who is on Hera's science team.

"We [could] measure its properties and say: 'Well, we need this mass of spacecraft, travelling at this speed, this early, in order to deflect it enough so that it misses the Earth'."

Hera's arrival on the scene is helping scientists answer many more questions too.

Not only did the collision alter the shape of Dimorphos, it also changed the way it moves.

"Before the Dart impact, Dimorphos was more like our own Moon - so it was always showing the same face to Didymos, and it was behaving quite nicely," explained Raducan.

"Now it's very, very chaotic - it's tumbling. Imagine a barrel that you throw down the stairs, and the barrel is rolling and it's moving, and basically that's what Dimorphos does right now around Didymos."

Hera has also taken detailed images of Didymos, revealing its surface in detail.

"The gravity at the surface of Didymos is about 40,000 times less than the gravity on Earth," said Naomi Murdoch, who is on the Hera mission team.

"We can already see some fascinating and complex geology. We can see regions of boulders.

"The smallest details that we can make out in these images are about 3m in size. So that means that all the boulders that you can see with your eyes are at least 3m big, and some as big as 10m. So what we're seeing here is boulders the size of cars and buses sitting on a world with almost no gravity."

The Hera mission will spend the next six months studying Dimorphos and Didymos, sending back more images taken from closer up in higher resolution.

"Hera is a sort of Inspector Columbo going back to the crash scene to investigate what is the outcome of this impact," said Patrick Michel, principal investigator of ESA's Hera mission.

The spacecraft is packed with instruments and also has two shoe-boxed sized satellites onboard, which can study the impact site up close, and then later land on the asteroid.

But the first images taken by Hera have also revealed a new challenge. Dimorphos and Didymos are travelling through space surrounded by hundreds of boulders ranging in size from tens of centimetres to metre-size rocks.

This will make it especially challenging to operate the spacecraft and cube satellites through this boulder field.

Asteroids pose a significant threat to our planet.

The biggest, which measures more than a kilometre across, could cause global devastation. But medium-sized asteroids around the same dimensions as Dimorphos could wipe out a city.

"We all know what happened to the dinosaurs, right? And we don't want that to happen to us," said Carolyn Ernst at Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory, who has worked on both the Dart and Hera missions.

"The good news for us is that there are far fewer potential threats out there in the Solar System than there were millions of years ago. But there are objects out there."

She said the biggest asteroids have been spotted, and none are heading to Earth.

"The smallest stuff isn't too much of a threat because our atmosphere protects us," she added.

"But there's a size range in the middle where we don't know where all of them are, and it could, if impacted, cause problems for humanity. And if we can find out about that and know about that, well, we sure as heck would want to try to stop that."

Scientists want to gather as much intelligence as they can about space rocks to make us as well equipped as possible to deal with whatever the Universe throws at us.

A new mission is launching in 2027 to track potentially hazardous asteroids - a space telescope called the Near-Earth Object (NEO) Surveyor.

There are also more visits planned to asteroids, including to one called Apophis, which is about 450m (1,480ft) long.

Apophis was discovered in 2004 and it was initially thought it might hit the Earth as early as 13 April 2029.

But now scientists understand its orbit better, and say it won't hit us for at least the next 100 years. Instead of a crash in 2029, it will fly just 32,000km (20,000 miles) above our surface.

This will give scientists the rare chance to study a space rock up-close.

Two spacecraft will head to Apophis, including Nasa's Osiris-Apex (which previously grabbed a sample from another asteroid called Bennu) and Ramses, a joint mission between ESA and the Japanese Space Agency (JAXA).

articles.title: EPA reports ‘zero’ airborne lead following controlled Army detonation in Iowa
articles.summary: The EPA said air monitors show zero detection of airborne lead in the region surrounding Middletown, IA, where the Army detonated a lead azide stockpile.
articles.body: Saying it was necessary to prevent the possible spontaneous explosion of a stockpile of material used in igniters and blasting caps, the US Army conducted a controlled detonation of over 9,700 pounds of lead azide today at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP) in Middletown, Iowa. Videos of the detonation showed plumes of smoke several hundred feet high drifting south before quickly dissipating. Following the explosion, the Army confirmed that all of the barrels at the plant had been destroyed without any secondary explosions or infrastructure damage. “I believe, absolutely, that we reduced, as close to zero as it’s absolutely humanly possible, the risk to the health and safety of the people of Middletown and the extended communities throughout Iowa,” said Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley during a press conference held two hours after the blast, according to the Associated Press. The US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has been monitoring the area around the ammunition plant leading up to today’s event. According to a statement from the EPA following the detonation, “real-time air monitors are reporting zero detection of airborne lead throughout the region” an hour after the detonation. The data collected by EPA employees, contractors, and monitoring equipment is shared here. The Army has used lead azide in munitions for nearly a century but began transitioning away from the material around 15 years ago because it can be difficult to transport and store. Over time, the material can degrade and crystallize and eventually become unstable enough to detonate at ambient temperatures. The Iowa ammunition plant housed 68 barrels containing about 9,700 pounds of lead azide, representing the country’s remaining stockpile. For safety reasons, the material was stored in liquid form embedded in sawdust and burlap bags while water and ethanol were added to prevent freezing. However, the decision was made to detonate the stockpile after an inspection by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms (ATF) discovered “significant crystallization on the exterior of the barrels” last March. Ahead of today’s detonation, the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) supported a recommended, but voluntary, temporary relocation of all the residents of Middletown and immediate surrounding areas that began yesterday. A cone-shaped evacuation zone extends about five miles southwest of the ammunition plant to account for the post-explosion dispersion and deposition path of dust. Displaced residents will be lodged until Friday, November 27th, and can return home once the all-clear has been given. To reduce the amount of lead dust released into surrounding areas and the environment, the Army said it took several additional precautions as part of today’s detonation. Walls made of four 16,000-gallon water tanks were installed to capture lead particulate, while the aging earth-covered magazines holding the barrels were covered with tarps and lead containment screens and flooded with foam.

articles.title: SpaceX gets green light to deploy 1 million satellites for data centers in space
articles.summary: The Federal Communications Commission is authorizing Elon Musk’s SpaceX to deploy a constellation of 1 million satellites for data centers in space, the agency said.
articles.body: The Federal Communications Commission is authorizing Elon Musk’s SpaceX to deploy a constellation of 1 million satellites for data centers in space, the agency said on Wednesday. SpaceX earlier this year sought permission to deploy up to 1 million orbital compute modules to process massive amounts of data to be used on Earth. The FCC said it was approving the SpaceX “Starmind” constellation to help meet rapidly growing demand for AI computing. Under the license, SpaceX must begin deployment no later than November 2033, deploy 10% of the maximum number — or 100,000 — no later than November 2035 and deploy 50% by November 2038, the FCC said. Approving the application will permit SpaceX “to pioneer emergent technology that advances American leadership in space and artificial intelligence,” the FCC added. Data centers are the physical backbone of artificial intelligence, requiring massive amounts of power. “By directly harnessing near-constant solar power with little operating or maintenance costs, these satellites will achieve transformative cost and energy efficiency while significantly reducing the environmental impact associated with terrestrial data centers,” SpaceX told the FCC. It was unclear whether SpaceX would put 1 million satellites in space, where only 17,000 satellites exist currently. Satellite operators sometimes request approval for higher numbers of satellites than they intend to deploy to buy design flexibility. SpaceX sought approval for 42,000 Starlink satellites before it began deployment of that system. The growing network currently has just over 11,000 satellites in space. SpaceX’s request bets heavily on reduced costs of Starship, the company’s next-generation reusable rocket under development, to help deploy satellites. Amazon’s rival satellite unit Leo and others have criticized the plan, suggesting SpaceX was unlikely to deploy all the satellites and that it could take centuries to do so. FCC Chair Brendan Carr rejected that criticism in March. “Amazon should focus on getting Amazon’s house in order with their own launches and their own satellite constellation, rather than worrying about other people that are actually out there ​launching satellites at the pace and cadence that SpaceX is,” Carr said. The FCC said it was also approving SpaceX’s requests to back up its optical network by approving additional communications.

articles.body:
The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) approved Elon Musk’s plan for his company SpaceX to launch up to 1 million orbital data centers into space, citing a need to meet growing AI computing demand.

FCC Chair Brendan Carr said in a statement that “by moving compute capacity beyond Earth, SpaceX and the many competitors working on their own orbital data centers are meeting the moment.”

“This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home,” Carr continued.

He added that “compute campuses or data centers are essential to sustaining America’s leadership in” artificial intelligence.

The approval gives SpaceX a 15-year permit to accomplish its goals of launching 1 million data centers. The firm must launch its first station into orbit by Nov. 25, 2033, with more deadlines outlined until 2040.

The FCC chair expressed on social media Wednesday that this was the first time the agency had authorized a permit for 1 million orbital data centers, which are set to be arranged in a constellation called “Starmind.”

Musk responded to Carr’s post , writing, “Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world.”

Data centers have quickly lost favor among Americans, with many cities across the country voting against approving projects or permits for the computing infrastructure in November’s midterm elections. Amid the growing dissatisfaction, Musk’s SpaceX and other tech firms began experimenting with launching orbital data centers that relied on solar power to fuel its computing.

Musk stated earlier this year that putting data centers in space could also work as a potential solution to the rising energy demands of AI.

Jared Isaacman, administrator of NASA, signaled his support for the idea in August, saying the move would “have immense benefits,” as companies could leverage solar energy to power data centers.

“Let’s take our data centers, put them in Earth orbit, take advantage of that free fusion reactor that’s out there for us and use that to ensure we do win the … space race for sure, but the AI race, too,” Isaacman said in an interview with Vinay Simlot, Nexstar Media Group’s Washington, D.C., correspondent.

SpaceX did not respond immediately to The Hill’s request for comment.

articles.summary: The FCC dismissed some of the key concerns raised by opponents, including potential threats to scientific research, because the agency determined they fell outside its regulatory authority.
articles.body:
SpaceX was given conditional approval by the Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday to deploy and operate a constellation of up to 1 million satellites for its orbital data center business, a regulatory victory for Elon Musk and his bid to move AI data centers into space.

The FCC authorization was granted despite objections from Amazon, Viasat, and the American Astronomical Society, which flagged concerns over orbital debris and congestion, radiofrequency interference, and environmental consequences. Amazon, which is building a competitor to SpaceX’s Starlink service, argued in its petition that the application lacked basic details and described it as a “lofty ambition rather than a real plan.” Despite that lack of detail, Amazon also said the proposal “risks real harm.”

The FCC dismissed some of the key concerns raised by opponents, including potential threats to scientific research, because the agency determined they fell outside its regulatory authority.

FCC Chair Brendan Carr said in a statement that the action “opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth.”

Musk thanked Carr in a post on X , writing “Much appreciate. This will be a great asset to America and the world.”

This initial regulatory approval doesn’t mean orbital data centers are imminent.

SpaceX faces a number of technical and economic challenges, including how to dramatically reduce the cost of manufacturing and launching satellites, cool processors in space, and even how to secure financing for chips that are destined for orbit.

The company must also clear other regulatory hurdles. The FCC has not yet approved SpaceX’s plans to handle orbital debris for satellites that would operate above 600 kilometers, for instance. SpaceX requested a waiver of existing FCC rules, which requires satellites ending missions below 2,000 kilometers reenter Earth’s atmosphere within five years of completing those missions. The company is interested in moving some of these retired satellites into other orbits around Earth or even around the sun, according to the FCC authorization document .

SpaceX has said it plans to deploy the satellites, known as Starmind, at altitudes ranging from 500 to 1,002 kilometers. The FCC’s approval gives SpaceX the authority to use radiofrequency communications to maintain contact with and control its orbital data centers from Earth if their primary communications systems fail. The Starmind satellites would primarily communicate using lasers to connect with other satellites, including SpaceX’s Starlink.

The FCC has given SpaceX time to sort out these issues. Under the approval, SpaceX has seven years to get its first operational satellite into orbit and 14 years to deploy the entire constellation.

articles.title: Researchers analyse DNA from 1,313 ancient people spanning 37,000 years, revealing how infectious diseases spread across Eurasia
articles.summary: Scientists have traced the presence and spread of infectious pathogens across 37,000 years of Eurasian history by examining DNA data from 1,313 ancient
articles.body: Scientists have traced the presence and spread of infectious pathogens across 37,000 years of Eurasian history by examining DNA data from 1,313 ancient people. The study identified thousands of traces of bacteria, viruses, and parasites, including many known human pathogens that had not previously been found in ancient human remains.According to research published in Nature, titled “The spatiotemporal distribution of human pathogens in ancient Eurasia”, the rise in zoonotic pathogens is thought to have occurred after animal husbandry pastoralism became widespread. The study maps pathogen diversity across Eurasia. The analysis detected 5,486 microbial DNA hits across 492 species from 136 genera, with 3,384 hits involving known human pathogens.Researchers examined DNA from 1,313 ancient individuals across EurasiaThe researchers screened shotgun-sequencing data from 1,313 ancient individuals, covering western Eurasia, central and north Asia, and southeast Asia. The samples spanned roughly 37,000 years, from the Upper Palaeolithic to historical times. The dataset contained about 405 billion sequencing reads. The team identified 5,486 authenticated microbial DNA hits across 1,005 samples. These included 3,384 hits among 214 known human pathogen species and 2,104 hits involving 278 other species.The detected material included bacterial, viral, and parasite DNA. Many of the human pathogens had not previously been identified in ancient human remains. The researchers noted that burial practices varied across cultures and periods, meaning the samples represented only some groups within past societies. They used a high-throughput computational workflow for screening.Ancient DNA revealed evidence of plague, leprosy and other infectionsThe study identified several pathogens across ancient Eurasia, including the bacterium Yersinia pestis, which causes plague. Researchers reported 42 putative cases, 35 of them newly identified, with the earliest three dating to around 5,700 to 5,300 calibrated years before present. The cases came from Western Russia, Central Asia, and Lake Baikal in Siberia.The team also reported 34 new putative cases of Borrelia recurrentis, the bacterium responsible for louse-borne relapsing fever. Its earliest identified case came from a Neolithic farmer in Scandinavia. 7 individuals carried the leprosy-causing bacterium Mycobacterium leprae. The researchers also detected putative cases of yersiniosis, leptospirosis, diphtheria, malaria and hepatitis B. They identified 28 hepatitis B virus cases, including cases from Mesolithic and Neolithic contexts in Siberia.How did animal husbandry influence the spread of ancient diseasesThe researchers found that zoonotic pathogens were not detected in their dataset until around 6,500 years ago. Their detection rates increased from roughly 6,000 years ago and remained elevated until the medieval period. The findings coincided with the widespread adoption of animal husbandry and pastoralism. According to the researchers, lifestyle changes probably increased the risk and extent of zoonotic transmission.They also found increased detection rates for pathogens transmitted between people from around 2,500 years ago. The study reported that species associated with the ancient oral microbiome accounted for up to 50% of ancient microbial hits across different periods. Environmental microbial species were detected at consistent rates, while infection-related groups generally had lower detection rates.Plague and relapsing fever spread at different times in ancient EurasiaThe researchers also examined changes in plague and louse-borne relapsing fever over time. Plague detection began rising around 6,000 years ago and reached an initial peak roughly 5,000 years ago across Europe and the Eurasian Steppe. Louse-borne relapsing fever showed an early peak around 5,500 years ago, then became more consistently detectable from roughly 2,800 years ago.According to the researchers, the spread of zoonotic pathogens increased substantially in later millennia, coinciding with pastoralist migrations from the Eurasian Steppe. The study acknowledged that ancient DNA analysis can miss infections when pathogen levels are low, or the sampled tissue is unsuitable.Fearless legend or grounded realist?
